name: quiche
summary: A Rust implementation of QUIC and HTTP/3 that keeps packet processing and connection state in a low-level library while delegating sockets, timers, and event-loop integration to the application.

features.name: Application-driven packet engine
features.description: quiche exposes connection methods that process received packets and generate outgoing packets, while the embedding application supplies sockets, packet I/O, an event loop, and timers.
benefits: Keeps the protocol core independent of a particular socket or async runtime
Allows applications to integrate QUIC progress with existing event loops
costs: Applications must correctly provide I/O, timer, pacing, and retry driving
Incorrect event-loop integration can prevent protocol progress

features.name: Configured connection state
features.description: A shared Config establishes the QUIC version, ALPN identifiers, stream and connection flow-control limits, congestion-control algorithm, idle timeout, and TLS settings used to create client or server connections.
benefits: Concentrates transport and security policy before connection creation
Allows one configuration to be reused across multiple connections
costs: Applications must choose limits appropriate to their workload
Configuration errors can surface only when a connection is created or driven

features.name: Stream-multiplexed transport
features.description: The QUIC connection exposes independent bidirectional and unidirectional streams for ordered application bytes, with per-stream and connection-level flow control and stream reset operations.
benefits: Allows concurrent application exchanges within one connection
Bounds sender progress through stream and connection credit
costs: Out-of-order packet delivery requires buffering until stream offsets can be reassembled
Stream and connection limits constrain concurrency and memory use

features.name: TLS-integrated handshake
features.description: quiche integrates TLS configuration and handshake progress into QUIC connection state; the application negotiates the application protocol through ALPN and drives the resulting encrypted packet exchange.
benefits: Combines transport establishment and authenticated key negotiation
Provides confidentiality and integrity for QUIC packets
costs: TLS configuration and certificate policy remain deployment responsibilities
Handshake failures cross the transport and cryptographic boundaries

features.name: HTTP/3 over QUIC module
features.description: The h3 module builds an HTTP/3 connection over a QUIC transport, opens control and QPACK streams during setup, and exposes request, response, body, and event polling APIs over QUIC streams.
benefits: Maps HTTP request/response exchanges onto independent QUIC streams
Provides QPACK and HTTP/3 frame processing above the transport core
costs: HTTP/3 setup depends on a suitable QUIC state and stream capacity
QPACK state and blocked header processing add ordering and resource concerns

features.name: Loss recovery and pacing boundary
features.description: quiche generates retransmission and congestion-control work through connection state and exposes timeout and pacing information for the application to schedule subsequent packet transmission.
benefits: Preserves reliable stream delivery over UDP datagrams
Makes timer and pacing decisions observable to the host integration
costs: Reliable progress depends on the host honoring timeout and pacing signals
Loss recovery and congestion control add state and scheduling complexity

mathematical_views.question: How does a quiche connection move from configuration and handshake through packet processing, stream service, timeout work, and termination?
assumptions: A connection is a stateful endpoint whose transitions are driven by application calls, received packets, and timer events
The view describes protocol behavior and does not prove liveness under arbitrary host scheduling

mathematical_views.question: Which operations must occur in order for an embedding application to establish QUIC and then exchange HTTP/3 data?
assumptions: Configuration precedes connection creation, packet receive/send driving, and HTTP/3 connection setup
HTTP/3 control and QPACK streams are established before normal request events are processed
The graph models ordering constraints rather than a single event-loop implementation

mathematical_views.question: How do connection, stream, header, and QPACK limits bound protocol resource consumption?
assumptions: Connection-level limits aggregate stream data and stream counts
Per-stream limits prevent one stream from consuming the whole receive budget
Header and QPACK limits are implementation policies and do not establish a universal memory bound

mathematical_views.question: Which layers can evolve independently while retaining a compatible QUIC and HTTP/3 integration boundary?
assumptions: QUIC version negotiation, ALPN, HTTP/3 settings, and extension frame rules are explicit compatibility surfaces
The view identifies candidate evolution boundaries and is not a claim that all versions interoperate

benefits: Runtime-neutral integration with explicit packet and timer control
costs: The host application owns correctness of I/O and event-loop driving

benefits: Centralized transport, security, and resource policy
costs: Workload-specific settings make connection setup policy-heavy

benefits: Independent concurrent streams over one secure connection
costs: Buffering, flow-control, and stream lifecycle state grow with concurrency

benefits: Authenticated encryption is part of transport establishment
costs: TLS policy and transport failure handling must be coordinated

benefits: HTTP/3 semantics reuse QUIC multiplexing and security
costs: HTTP/QPACK state adds another protocol layer and error surface

benefits: Reliable delivery and congestion response over UDP
costs: Timer, pacing, retransmission, and congestion state require host cooperation
